It is the “Command Line Interface Composition Kit”: highly configurable, with sensible defaults. It exists so that writing command line tools is quick, and so that an intended command-line API can actually be implemented — including arbitrary nesting of commands — rather than being blocked by the parser.\n\nOptlyn in three points, as the product itself states them:\n\n- Arbitrary nesting of commands\n- Automatic help page generation\n- Support for lazy loading of subcommands at runtime\n\nThe finished product is a **library**, not a command users type. An application author declares commands, groups, options, and arguments; Optlyn parses the process argument list, converts values, generates help, dispatches to the author’s callbacks, and supplies terminal helpers. End users of those applications see a POSIX-style command line: options, positional arguments, nested subcommands, and a help page.\n\nThis document specifies **user- and integrator-observable behavior only**. Exact published symbol names, import paths, and decorator spellings belong in the Interface Contract, not here. Every feature point below corresponds to behavior that exists in the finished product. Feature points are ordered so foundational capabilities come first; a later feature point may refine an earlier one only when it says so explicitly.\n\n## Terminology\n\n| Term | Meaning in this PRD |\n| --- | --- |\n| **Command** | A callable unit that parses a slice of the command line and runs an author-supplied callback. A bare command is a leaf: it has options and arguments, but no nested subcommands. |\n| **Group** | A command that dispatches to named subcommands (which may themselves be groups). Groups are how Optlyn nests CLIs. |\n| **Option** | A named parameter, typically introduced by a dash prefix (`-` or `--`, or another declared prefix). Options are optional unless the author marks them required. They appear fully on the help page. |\n| **Argument** | A positional parameter. Arguments are the usual place for files, URLs, and leftover tokens. They are not fully documented on the help page unless the author supplies help text or documents them in the command’s description. |\n| **Parameter** | An option or an argument. |\n| **Invocation context** | The per-invocation state Optlyn creates when a command runs: parsed values, parent/child linkage, an optional author object, resource cleanup, and flags that affect parsing and output. |\n| **Help page** | The usage text Optlyn generates for a command or group when the user asks for help, or when a group is invoked incorrectly under the default “no arguments means help” policy. Layout is Optlyn’s; wording of descriptions is the author’s. |\n| **Callback** | The author function attached to a command, group, or parameter. Command callbacks receive converted parameter values. Parameter callbacks receive the converted value and may replace it or refuse it. A parameter callback is not called for a parameter that was omitted and received no value from any source. |\n| **Eager parameter** | A parameter that can finish the invocation even when other required parameters are still missing. Help and version flags are eager. If several eager flags appear, the one the user typed first is the one that takes effect. |\n| **Default map** | A nested mapping of parameter defaults supplied on the invocation context, used to override declared defaults (for example from a config file) without changing the command definition. |\n| **Chaining group** | A group that runs several subcommands in one invocation, in the order they appear on the command line. |\n| **Interactive session** | A run whose standard input is attached to a terminal (PTY), or whose standard input or standard output is a TTY. A piped standard input without a terminal is not interactive. |\n\n## Public surface inventory\n\nOptlyn is imported and used from Python. The public surface, grouped by feature point, is:\n\n- Declaring a function as a command or a group, attaching options and arguments, registering subcommands immediately or later, and invoking the result as a program or as an in-process call.\n- Automatic help (default `--help`) and an eager version flag that prints a version identity and exits, including a variant whose identity text is produced by an author callback.\n- Built-in parameter types, listed under FP-05; custom types the author supplies.\n- Prompts (option-integrated and standalone), confirmation, and hidden password input, including the ready-made password and confirmation option combinations.\n- File and path parameters, including `-` as stdin/stdout for the file type.\n- Terminal helpers: echo (including to standard error), styling, styled echo, stripping styles, pager output, progress bars, single-character input, pause-until-key, editor launch, application launch, screen clear, application-config directory lookup, filename formatting, text wrapping, and opening files or standard streams.\n- Shell completion for Bash (4.4 and newer), Zsh, Fish, and PowerShell, in both registration-script mode and suggestion-emission mode.\n- Usage-failure and abort handling with distinct exit-status classes.\n- An in-process runner that invokes a command with argument tokens and captures output and exit status.\n\nFeature points below group these entries by capability. They do not invent additional product surfaces. Packaging an application as a console-script entry point is how authors ship tools; it is not itself a Optlyn command.\n\n## Non-functional constraints\n\n- **Form factor:** A pure-Python library. Authors build CLIs with it; Optlyn is not a single end-user binary. The importable package directory is `optlyn` under `src`.\n- **Language:** Python 3.10 or newer. The package has zero declared runtime dependencies. Importing the package performs no I/O, starts no processes, and opens no sockets.\n- **Platforms:** Intended to work on Linux, macOS, and Windows. The supported target is Linux with a supported Python interpreter. No compiled extensions, native code, GPU, or accelerator are required or claimed. (On Windows, when invoked as a program, glob, home-directory, and environment tokens in the process argument list are expanded unless the author disables that; a Unix shell already expands before the process starts.)\n- **Hardware:** CPU-only.\n- **Parsing conventions:** Optlyn implements POSIX-style option parsing (short-option stacking, `--` to end option parsing, long options with `--`). Alternative option prefixes such as `/` and `+` are supported when the author declares them. Leaf commands, by default, also allow an option to appear after a positional argument; groups, by default, do not mix the group’s own options with the subcommand name (FP-03).\n- **Help layout:** Description text is customizable; the help **layout** is not a free-form author template. Nested Optlyn programs keep a consistent help shape when composed.\n- **Unicode:** Command-line values are text. Echo and file helpers exist so misconfigured terminals do not fail on ordinary Unicode output. An ASCII-only environment encoding does not abort invocation (FP-11).\n- **Threading:** The current invocation context is available on the thread that is running the command. Other threads do not see that context unless the author enters the same context in that thread. The context is not a thread-safe mutable store.\n\n## Non-goals\n\n- Being a general-purpose argument parser unrelated to command dispatch (Optlyn both parses and dispatches).\n- Letting authors fully redesign help-page layout (wording yes; layout no).\n- Shipping a remote server, GUI, or web framework.\n- Built-in command aliases or plugin discovery. Those are extension patterns authors implement on top of groups; they are not built-in commands of Optlyn itself. FP-06 requires that custom groups *can* resolve names their own way, not that a particular alias scheme ships.\n- A configuration-file syntax of Optlyn’s own. A default map can be loaded from whatever the author chooses.\n- Thread-safe mutation of an invocation context.\n- Guaranteeing color on every Windows console without extra platform support; recent Windows supports ANSI styling, and echo strips styles when the stream is not a terminal.\n\n---\n\n## Feature points\n\n### FP-01: Command declaration, naming, and invocation\n\n**Public entry:** Optlyn’s command declaration (applied to an ordinary Python function) and invoking the resulting command as a program — by calling it, by running it as a script, or as an installed console script. A group’s command-registration helper is also an entry for attaching a leaf command (FP-06).\n\n**Normal behavior:**\n\n- Decorating a function with no extra arguments produces a command whose name is the function name converted to lowercase, with underscores replaced by dashes, and with a trailing `_command`, `_cmd`, `_group`, or `_grp` suffix stripped when present. Passing an explicit name uses that name instead, and then only that name is accepted: the name derived from the function is not.\n- Invoking the command with a valid argument list runs the function once and returns a successful process exit when used as a program. The function body is the command’s work: whatever it writes appears, and it is not run more than once.\n- A command marked deprecated still runs and still succeeds. On invocation, Optlyn emits a deprecation warning on standard output, ahead of the command’s own output, that is distinguishable from ordinary command output and from a usage failure. A custom deprecation note, when the author supplies one, appears in that warning; the command does not refuse to run merely because it is deprecated. An unknown option on a deprecated command is still a usage error.\n- Parameters declared on the command are converted and passed into the function under the destination names inferred or declared for those parameters (FP-03). A command with no parameters still runs when invoked with an empty extra-argument list. Creating a command or group moves declarations previously attached to the function onto the new command and removes them from the function; decorating the same function again starts from an empty declaration list.\n- When the command is invoked as a standalone program, Optlyn handles the failure classes in FP-13 and exits the process. When the integrator disables standalone program mode, failures propagate to the caller and the command’s return value is available to the caller instead of being discarded.\n\n**Boundary / error behavior:**\n\n- Unknown option tokens, missing required parameters, and values that fail conversion do not run the command callback. They fail as usage errors (FP-13).\n- An ASCII-only environment encoding does not abort execution: the same command still runs and produces the same successful outcome as in a Unicode locale.\n- Leftover tokens beyond the declared arity that no variadic argument collects are a usage error, unless the command is configured to allow extra arguments. With extra arguments allowed, leftover tokens that are not option-shaped are tolerated and the callback runs; each declared argument still receives only the tokens that fill its own arity. An option-shaped leftover token (a leading dash, not after `--`) remains a usage error under that setting alone; consuming it as an argument requires the ignore-unknown-options setting (FP-03) or a preceding `--`.\n\n---\n\n### FP-02: Automatic help pages and eager documentation flags\n\n**Public entry:** The automatic help option on every command (default `--help`, overridable through the invocation context’s help-option names); the command’s docstring and per-option / per-argument help text; the ready-made version option and the ready-made custom-version option; optional epilog, short-help override, metavar, show-default, and show-environment-variable switches.\n\n**Normal behavior:**\n\n- Asking for help on a command prints a help page and does **not** run the command callback. The page includes a usage line, the command’s description, and a documented options section. Intentional help exits successfully (exit status zero).\n- If the function has a docstring, that docstring is the command description, unless the author supplies an explicit help string. A form-feed character in the docstring truncates the help: text after that character is omitted from the help page; text before it remains. The form-feed character itself does not appear on the page.\n- Option help strings appear next to those options. Argument help, when the author supplies it, appears in a positional-arguments section; without it, that section does not carry the argument. Arguments may also be described in the docstring by name.\n- For subcommands listed on a group help page, the short help is the first sentence of the docstring by default, ellipsized if it cannot fit on one line at the wrap width, or an explicit short-help string when the author sets one (which then replaces the first sentence).\n- Group help lists subcommands, the group’s options, positional arguments, and an epilog when one is set. The epilog is printed at the end of the help page, after everything else on it.\n- The usage line brackets optional elements and leaves required elements unbracketed. A variadic argument is marked with a trailing ellipsis. The default options placeholder is bracketed and occupies its own place on the usage line, distinct from any argument placeholder; an author override of that placeholder is used as given, without added brackets. A group that can run without a subcommand also brackets the leading command token; a chaining group brackets the extra command-and-args unit as optional and repeatable.\n- Help text is rewrapped to the terminal width; a maximum content width that defaults to 80 columns and can be raised by the caller caps auto-detected width only, and an explicit caller-supplied terminal width is the wrap width as-is (whatever the maximum content width). Single newlines inside a paragraph are not preserved as hard breaks. A paragraph whose first line is only a backspace character is not rewrapped: subsequent lines of that paragraph keep their line breaks, and the backspace line itself is stripped from the rendered help.\n- The default metavar for an argument is the argument name in uppercase. For an option that takes a value, the default metavar is the type name in uppercase, unless that type supplies its own placeholder (a choice type does); for example, an integer option `--count` appears on the help page as `--count COUNT`; a flag or counting option has no metavar. Authors may override the usage-line options placeholder and per-parameter metavars; an author metavar replaces the type-name placeholder.\n- The help entry of an option whose type is a closed choice lists the allowed values; an option of the plain text type does not.\n- When show-default is enabled, the help page shows the default in that option’s entry. Show-default may be enabled per parameter or for the whole invocation via the context. The author may supply a custom default description, shown instead of the raw default value. For a single-option boolean flag whose default is off (false), that default remains hidden even if show-default is on; a flag whose default is on (true) shows it. When show-environment-variable is enabled, the associated environment variable name appears in that option’s entry; when disabled, it does not.\n- The help page of a deprecated command carries a deprecation mark that the page of an otherwise identical non-deprecated command does not.\n- Hidden options, hidden commands, and hidden groups are omitted from help (and from completion — FP-12) but remain invocable if the user types their names.\n- Help-option names default to `--help`. The invocation context may replace that list; the new names then print help and a name no longer in the list is an unknown option. If an author-declared option reuses every help-option name, the automatic help option is dropped and the author’s option wins; if it reuses only some of those names, the overlapping name runs the author’s option and the remaining names still print help. A parameter merely *named* `help` (for example a positional argument called `help`) does not disable automatic help: both keep working. Authors may also attach an extra help option that prints help and exits the same way as the automatic option; it does not remove the automatic one.\n- The ready-made version option is eager: it prints a version identity and exits without running the command callback, even when other required parameters are missing or present. If the author supplies the version string, the identity contains it. If the author does not supply it, Optlyn detects it from the installed distribution of the given package name; if that name is not an installed distribution, it is treated as an import name and the version of the distribution that provides that import is used. A module’s own version attribute is not consulted. The ready-made custom-version option is the same eager flag, except the whole printed identity is exactly the string returned by an author callback that receives the invocation context: that return value is printed as-is, not wrapped in the built-in package/prog/version template or any other surrounding label. If both help and version appear on the command line, whichever eager flag the user typed first wins and exits; the other’s output does not appear.\n\n**Boundary / error behavior:**\n\n- Help shown because the user invoked a group with no subcommand under the default “no arguments means help” policy is a **usage failure**, not a successful help request: the help page is printed, the group callback is not run (unless the group is configured to invoke without a command — FP-06), and the exit status is the usage-error class (FP-13), not zero.\n- Incorrect usage of a command that causes Optlyn to show help (missing subcommand, and similar no-args-is-help paths) likewise uses the usage-error exit class. Passing the help option explicitly uses the success exit class.\n- A command may disable automatic help. Then `--help` is an unknown option unless the author declared it (for example with an extra help option of that name, which restores it).\n\n---\n\n### FP-03: Options\n\n**Public entry:** Optlyn’s option declaration on a command or group. Ready-made combinations that are still options (password option, confirmation option) are specified under FP-08; the version option under FP-02.\n\n**Normal behavior:**\n\n- Declarations attached as options (or arguments) live on the function until a command or group is created from it: those declarations are then moved onto the new command and removed from the function. Decorating the same function again starts from an empty declaration list. Several options on one command are independent: each fills only its own destination.\n- An option is optional by default. If it is omitted and has no default, the callback receives an absent value. If a default is set, Optlyn infers the type from that default when the author does not set a type (FP-05). A default that is already of the converted type is delivered unchanged. A default may be a callable; that callable is invoked when no earlier value source produced a value.\n- One option may be declared with several names (a short name and a long name, and additional aliases) that all set the same destination. Long options use a double-dash prefix and may take a value as `--name=value` or `--name value`. Short options use a single dash and a single character. Single-character short flags may be stacked: a stack is equivalent to each flag given separately. If the last flag in a stack takes a value, that value may be the next token or attached directly after it, whether alone or at the end of a stack. Multi-character short names are not supported: a single-dash token of several characters is a stack of single-character flags, not one option.\n- When the author does not give a destination name, it is inferred from the declared option names: a name that is already a valid identifier wins; otherwise the first long name; otherwise the first short name. A leading dash prefix is stripped and remaining dashes become underscores.\n- On a leaf command, options and positional arguments may be mixed: an option after an argument is parsed the same as before it. On a group, mixing is off by default: the subcommand name ends that group’s own option parsing, so group options must appear before the subcommand name. Authors may enable mixing on a group, in which case a group option after the subcommand name is still delivered to the group and the subcommand still runs.\n- An option may be required. Then omitting it is a usage error and the callback does not run, unless another source (environment, automatic prefix, default map) supplies it.\n- Boolean flags: a flag declared as a flag, when omitted, yields false unless the author set a true default; when present, it yields true. After `--`, a token spelled like the flag is an argument, not the flag. An explicit on/off pair (declared with either prefix style) yields true for the on token and false for the off token. Several flags may share one destination as a feature-switch group: the callback receives the flag value of the winning flag (see value resolution below).\n- A counting option yields how many times it occurred (zero if omitted). Each flag in a stack counts.\n- A repeatable option may be given several times; the callback receives the sequence of values in command-line order. If it is omitted and has no default, the callback receives an empty tuple, not an absent value. A declared default for a repeatable option must be a sequence (list or tuple) of values, delivered as a tuple in that order when the option is omitted. A multi-value option takes a fixed number of tokens per occurrence (strictly positive; not “consume the rest”): it is delivered as an indexable sequence of that length, a following token is left for the next parameter, and too few tokens is a usage error. Combined with repetition, each occurrence takes that many tokens. A tuple type on an option sets that arity to the tuple length and converts each position with the corresponding inner type.\n- An option may take an optional value: the flag alone yields the author’s flag-value; the flag plus a token yields that token; omitting the flag entirely yields the default. (A value option without this form, given with no value, is a missing-value usage error.)\n- Authors may declare prefixes other than `-`, including `/` and `+`.\n- Environment variables: an option may name one variable or a list of names (first one set wins). Names are matched exactly and are not whitespace-trimmed as names. An absent variable, or a variable present with a truly empty value, is treated as not supplying a value (the next source wins). An environment value is converted with the option’s type and may satisfy a required option. For a repeatable or multi-value option, the type splits a non-empty variable’s string: default split is whitespace; file and path types split on the platform path separator (`:` on Unix), keeping left-to-right order.\n- For boolean flags, environment values are strings interpreted as follows after stripping surrounding whitespace and ignoring case. Activation: `true`, `1`, `yes`, `on`, `t`, `y`. Deactivation: `false`, `0`, `no`, `off`, `f`, `n`. A whitespace-only value strips to empty and deactivates. Any other non-empty string is a conversion usage error, not a silent deactivation. If the flag has a non-boolean flag-value, a variable whose text equals that flag-value also activates; recognized true/false tokens activate or deactivate as above; unrecognized and empty values are treated as unset (the next source wins), not as a usage error. A paired on/off option recognizes only the single environment name the author attached, not a magically derived negative name.\n- A value is filled from command line, then environment, then the default map on the invocation context (FP-07), then the parameter’s declared default; the first of those that produces a value wins. Those four, plus an interactive prompt when one ran (FP-08), are ranked from most explicit to least as: prompt, command line, environment, default map, declared default.\n- Feature-switch groups (several options sharing one destination): the option whose source is most explicit wins. Within the default tier, an explicit declared default beats an auto-derived default (bare boolean flags auto-derive default false). If still tied, the last declared option wins.\n- A parameter callback sees the invocation context, the parameter, and the converted value, and may replace the value or refuse it. A refusal is a usage error: non-zero usage-class exit, a message on standard error that distinguishes the failure from success, the command callback not run, and the refused value not delivered. Callbacks run for every source including environment, default map, and prompts. An eager flag can finish the invocation even when required non-eager options are missing; when it is not given, the missing required option is still a usage error. A missing parameter still runs its callback, so that callback can default from an earlier parameter’s value (the values already bound are readable on the context). A repeated parameter fires its callback once, with all gathered values.\n- A parameter may be hidden from the callback (not passed as a function argument) while still being parsed — used by help, version, and confirmation flags. Its name is still accepted on the command line.\n- A deprecated option still parses. A deprecation warning is emitted only when the user actually supplied that option, not when the value came only from a default.\n\n**Boundary / error behavior:**\n\n- An unknown option is a usage error, unless the command is configured to ignore unknown options, in which case option-like tokens may be consumed as arguments without `--`, and leftover option-like tokens become extra arguments that a variadic pass-through argument can collect (FP-04). Unknown long options are left intact. Unknown short options may be split: a known short flag inside a stack is consumed and the unknown rest of the stack stays leftover. An option-like token left over beyond the declared arity is still a usage error unless extra arguments are allowed (FP-01).\n- A missing value for an option that requires one is a usage error.\n- A bare string (or other non-sequence) default on a repeatable option is a usage error whose report identifies the option and says that it needs an iterable (sequence) default, so that report is distinct from the report for a missing required option; it is not treated as a sequence of characters and not as a single string element. Authors who want one default string must pass a one-element sequence.\n- A deprecated option cannot also be required, and cannot use a prompt. Declaring that combination is refused at declaration time.\n- Option values belonging to a command must appear after that command’s name and before a nested command name (FP-06). A help option before a subcommand name is help for the parent, not for the subcommand.\n\n---\n\n### FP-04: Positional arguments\n\n**Public entry:** Optlyn’s argument declaration on a command or group.\n\n**Normal behavior:**\n\n- An argument is positional and binds tokens in declaration order. A minimal argument (a destination name only) is required, has no default, and is text unless a type or default implies otherwise (an integer default infers integer conversion, as for options).\n- An argument may be marked optional, or given a default; then omitting it is not a usage error and the callback receives the default, or an absent value (neither a string nor a sequence) when there is none. A supplied token overrides a default. An argument may declare a fixed positive arity or a variadic arity (consume the rest). A unary argument is delivered as a scalar; any other arity is delivered as an indexable sequence. Too few tokens for a required fixed arity is a usage error. Variadic arity may be used at most once on a command; a second variadic argument is refused or never runs the callback. A variadic argument omitted yields an empty sequence unless it was marked required, in which case omitting it is a usage error.\n- After a `--` token, subsequent tokens are arguments even if they look like options; the `--` token itself is not delivered. Without it, option-shaped tokens are not arguments (FP-01, FP-03).\n- An argument declared on a group is delivered to the group callback; the next token after it is the subcommand name.\n- Arguments may read from environment variables only when the author names those variables explicitly (one name or a list; first set wins). There is no automatic environment prefix for arguments (that prefix applies to options — FP-07), and a variable merely named like the destination does not fill one. An absent or truly empty variable is treated as not supplying a value. An environment value may satisfy a required argument and is overridden by a command-line token. A non-empty variable for a non-unary argument is split the same way as for a multi-value option (FP-03); a unary argument keeps the whole value.\n- Argument help is optional. Without it, the help page’s main description is where authors document them; with it, a positional-arguments section lists them (FP-02). An author metavar is the argument’s placeholder on the usage line.\n\n**Boundary / error behavior:**\n\n- A missing required argument is a usage error that identifies that argument, and the callback does not run.\n- E","stderr":"","interrupted":false,"isImage":false,"noOutputExpected":false,"persistedOutputPath":"/logs/agent/sessions/projects/-app/154f0ed2-eb90-4a16-aad9-19c2b66a4638/tool-results/bkhftf9gb.txt","persistedOutputSize":90525},"tool_result_meta":[{"id":"toolu_01Ux1dahMuaN9ebxrsfdaGCs","permission_decision":{"decision":"accept","source":"config","reason_type":"mode"}}]}

What the library does with those inputs, and every default value that changes behaviour, is stated in the PRD. Wherever a form is not stated below, it is the implementer’s choice.\n\n## 1. Package and modules\n\n- Distribution and import package: `optlyn`, laid out as `src/optlyn`. Python 3.10 or newer, no runtime dependencies.\n- The package root `optlyn` exports these names (all importable as `from optlyn import <name>`):\n  - Declaration: `command`, `group`, `option`, `argument`, `help_option`, `version_option`, `custom_version_option`, `password_option`, `confirmation_option`, `pass_context`, `pass_obj`, `make_pass_decorator`.\n  - Classes: `Command`, `Group`, `CommandCollection`, `Context`, `Option`, `Parameter`, `ParamType`, `BadParameter`, `Abort`.\n  - Parameter types: `STRING`, `INT`, `FLOAT`, `BOOL`, `UUID`, `UNPROCESSED` (ready-made instances); `Choice`, `DateTime`, `IntRange`, `FloatRange`, `Tuple`, `File`, `Path` (constructible).\n  - Terminal helpers: `echo`, `secho`, `style`, `unstyle`, `echo_via_pager`, `get_pager_file`, `progressbar`, `prompt`, `confirm`, `getchar`, `pause`, `edit`, `launch`, `clear`, `get_app_dir`, `get_current_context`, `format_filename`, `open_file`.\n- `optlyn.testing` exports `CliRunner`.\n- `optlyn.formatting` exports `wrap_text`.\n- Further exports are the implementer’s choice.\n\n## 2. Global output forms\n\n### Exit statuses (standalone mode)\n\n| status | meaning |\n| --- | --- |\n| `0` | success, intentional help, version, or an author clean stop with no status |\n| `2` | usage error |\n| `1` | abort, or another library-signalled error that is not a usage error (including a file that fails to open at first I/O) |\n| `<n>` | an author clean stop with status `<n>` |\n\nStandalone mode ends the process with `SystemExit` carrying that status. With standalone mode off, the process is not exited: failures surface to the caller as raised exceptions, and the call returns the callback’s return value. Exception class names other than those listed in section 1 are the implementer’s choice.\n\n### Channels\n\n| output | channel |\n| --- | --- |\n| help page asked for intentionally | standard output |\n| help page shown because of incorrect usage (for example a group invoked with no subcommand) | standard error |\n| version identity | standard output |\n| usage-error report | standard error |\n| abort indication | standard error |\n| general error report (for example a file that cannot be opened at first I/O) | standard error |\n| deprecation warning for a command, option or argument | standard error |\n| completion registration script and suggestion stream | standard output |\n| prompt and confirmation question text | standard output |\n| progress bar, pause message, screen-clear sequence | standard output |\n\nWording of every report, warning and indication is the implementer’s choice, with these exceptions: a usage-error report about a parameter contains that parameter’s identity, which is one of the option’s declared flag names exactly as declared or the argument’s name (letter case is the implementer’s choice). A report about a path that cannot be opened or fails a path check contains that path. A custom deprecation note appears verbatim in the deprecation warning.\n\n### Help page\n\nPrinted on the channel given above. It contains, in this order:\n\n1. A usage line that contains the program name, the options placeholder (default spelling the implementer’s choice; an author `options_metavar` appears verbatim as its own whitespace-separated token), and each argument’s placeholder (its `metavar`, by default the argument name in uppercase).\n2. The command description.\n3. A section headed `Positional arguments` when at least one argument has `help`; each entry carries the argument’s placeholder and its help text.\n4. A section headed `Options`; each option’s entry is contiguous and starts with its declared names, followed by its metavar (if any) and its help text. Extras (shown default, environment variable name, choice values) follow inside that entry, in a form that is the implementer’s choice.\n5. For a group, a section that lists each visible child with its short help.\n6. The epilog, when set.\n\nSection ordering beyond the above, the deprecation mark, punctuation and indentation are the implementer’s choice.\n\n### Version identity\n\nThe version flag prints a single page on standard output. For `version_option` the page contains the version string, and the surrounding text is the implementer’s choice. For `custom_version_option` the page is exactly the callback’s returned string followed by a newline.\n\n## 3. Declaring commands and groups\n\n### `command`\n\n```\ncommand(name=None, cls=None, **attrs)\n```\n\n- Used as `@command()` or `@command` on a function. It returns a command instance (a `Command`, or an instance of `cls`).\n- `name`: the exported name (`str`), or `None` to derive it from the function.\n- `attrs` keywords accepted: `help` (description text), `short_help`, `epilog`, `options_metavar`, `context_settings` (mapping, see `Context`), `add_help_option` (bool), `no_args_is_help` (bool), `deprecated` (bool, or a `str` note), `hidden` (bool).\n\nCommand instance members:\n\n- `main(args=None, prog_name=None, complete_var=None, standalone_mode=True, **extra)`: runs the command. `args` is a list of tokens, and `None` means `sys.argv[1:]`. `prog_name` is the program name shown on usage lines and used to derive the completion variable, and `None` derives it from the process. `complete_var` replaces the derived completion-variable name. `extra` keywords go to the invocation `Context`.\n- Calling the instance (`cmd(...)`) is `main(...)`.\n- `callback`: the author function.\n- `params`: the list of declared parameter objects.\n\n### `group`\n\n```\ngroup(name=None, cls=None, **attrs)\n```\n\n- Used as `@group()` or `@group`. It returns a group instance (a `Group`, or an instance of `cls`).\n- `attrs` keywords accepted are those of `command`, plus `chain` (bool), `invoke_without_command` (bool), and, when `cls=CommandCollection`, `sources` (a list of groups).\n\n### `Group`\n\n```\nGroup(name=None, commands=None, invoke_without_command=False, no_args_is_help=None, subcommand_metavar=None, chain=False, result_callback=None, **kwargs)\n```\n\n- `no_args_is_help=None` means “derive it from `invoke_without_command`”, as stated in the PRD.\n- A subclass may be passed as `cls` to `group`. The instance is then of that subclass, and the subclass receives the same constructor arguments.\n- Members:\n  - `add_command(cmd, name=None)`: registers `cmd` under `name`, or under the command’s own name when `name` is `None`. Attaching a group beneath a chaining group raises at that call.\n  - `command(*args, **kwargs)` and `group(*args, **kwargs)`: the same arguments as the root decorators. The decorated child is registered on this group.\n  - `result_callback()`: returns a decorator. The decorated function is called as `f(value, **group_params)`, where `value` is a list of child returns (chain mode) or the single return (non-chain mode).\n  - `list_commands(ctx) -> list[str]` and `get_command(ctx, cmd_name) -> Command | None`: listing and lookup. These are the override points for custom groups.\n  - `callback`: the group’s author function.\n\n### `CommandCollection`\n\n```\nCommandCollection(name=None, sources=None, **kwargs)\n```\n\nA `Group` subclass. `sources` is a list of groups, and `None` means an empty list. It is normally built as `group(cls=CommandCollection, sources=[...])(callback)`.\n\n## 4. Parameters\n\n### `option`\n\n```\noption(*param_decls, cls=None, **attrs)\n```\n\n- `param_decls`: names starting with a prefix character are flag names (`<prefix><prefix><long>` or `<prefix><c>`, where `<prefix>` is `-` or another declared prefix character). A declaration of the form `<on-flag>/<off-flag>` declares an on/off pair. A name with no prefix is the destination.\n- It returns a decorator that attaches the option and returns the function.\n- `attrs` keywords accepted:\n\n| keyword | meaning |\n| --- | --- |\n| `type` | a parameter type instance, a `ParamType` subclass instance, or a conversion function `f(token) -> value` that refuses by raising `ValueError` |\n| `default` | a value, or a zero-argument callable |\n| `required` | bool |\n| `is_flag` | bool |\n| `flag_value` | the value delivered when the flag is present |\n| `count` | bool: counting option |\n| `multiple` | bool: repeatable |\n| `nargs` | positive int: tokens per occurrence |\n| `envvar` | `str` or list of `str` |\n| `allow_from_autoenv` | bool |\n| `prompt` | bool, or a `str` question |\n| `prompt_required` | bool |\n| `hide_input` | bool |\n| `confirmation_prompt` | bool |\n| `callback` | `f(ctx, param, value) -> value`; refuses by raising `BadParameter` |\n| `is_eager` | bool |\n| `expose_value` | bool |\n| `hidden` | bool |\n| `deprecated` | bool, or a `str` note |\n| `help` | text |\n| `metavar` | text |\n| `show_default` | bool, or a `str` shown instead of the value |\n| `show_envvar` | bool |\n| `shell_complete` | `f(ctx, param, incomplete)`; see section 8 |\n\nAn invalid combination of keywords (as the PRD defines) raises at declaration, when the decorator is applied.\n\n### `argument`\n\n```\nargument(*param_decls, cls=None, **attrs)\n```\n\n- `param_decls`: a single destination name.\n- `attrs` keywords accepted: `type`, `default`, `required`, `nargs` (positive int, or `-1` for variadic), `envvar`, `deprecated`, `help`, `metavar`. An invalid combination raises at declaration.\n\n### Delivered values\n\nThe command callback is called with keyword arguments named by the parameter destinations.\n\n| case | value delivered |\n| --- | --- |\n| unary parameter | a scalar |\n| `nargs` other than 1, or a `Tuple` type | a tuple |\n| `multiple=True` | a tuple, one entry per occurrence |\n| omitted variadic argument or repeatable option | `()` |\n| omitted parameter with no value from any source | `None` |\n| flag | a `bool`, or its `flag_value` |\n| counting option | an `int` |\n\n### Parameter objects\n\n`Option` and the argument class are `Parameter` subclasses. Parameter callbacks and completion functions receive these objects. Each exposes `name` (the destination) and `metavar` (the author string, or `None` when not given).\n\n### Ready-made option decorators\n\n| signature | default flag name | what it attaches |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| `help_option(*param_decls, **kwargs)` | | an extra eager help flag |\n| `version_option(version=None, *param_decls, package_name=None, prog_name=None, message=None, **kwargs)` | `--version` | an eager version flag |\n| `custom_version_option(callback, *param_decls, **kwargs)` | `--version` | an eager version flag; `callback(ctx) -> str` |\n| `password_option(*param_decls, **kwargs)` | `--password` | a prompting, hidden, confirmed option |\n| `confirmation_option(*param_decls, **kwargs)` | `--yes` | a confirmation flag; `prompt=` sets the question text |\n\n- `help_option`: the declared names print the help page.\n- `version_option`: `version` is the identity, and `None` means it is detected via `package_name`.\n- `custom_version_option`: the identity is the string `callback(ctx)` returns.\n\n### `BadParameter`\n\n```\nBadParameter(message, ctx=None, param=None, param_hint=None)\n```\n\nRaised from a parameter callback, from a `ParamType.convert`, or from a conversion function, to refuse a value. `message` is text, and the remaining arguments are optional.\n\n## 5. Parameter types\n\n| entry | form |\n| --- | --- |\n| `STRING`, `INT`, `FLOAT`, `BOOL`, `UUID`, `UNPROCESSED` | ready-made instances. They deliver `str`, `int`, `float`, `bool`, `uuid.UUID`, and the raw token, respectively |\n| `Choice(choices, case_sensitive=True)` | `choices` is an iterable of values, or an `enum.Enum` subclass (members are matched by name) |\n| `DateTime(formats=None)` | `formats` is a sequence of `strftime` format strings, and `None` means the default list. Delivers `datetime.datetime` |\n| `IntRange(min=None, max=None, min_open=False, max_open=False, clamp=False)` | delivers `int` |\n| `FloatRange(min=None, max=None, min_open=False, max_open=False, clamp=False)` | delivers `float`. An invalid combination raises when constructed |\n| `Tuple(types)` | `types` is a sequence of types, one per position |\n| `File(mode=\"r\", encoding=None, errors=\"strict\", lazy=None, atomic=False)` | `mode` is one of `r`, `w`, `rb`, `wb`. `lazy=None` means the mode-dependent behaviour the PRD states. Delivers an open file object |\n| `Path(exists=False, file_okay=True, dir_okay=True, writable=False, readable=True, resolve_path=False, allow_dash=False, path_type=None, executable=False)` | `path_type` is `str`, `pathlib.Path`, or `None` (deliver `str`). Delivers a path, not an open file |\n| `ParamType` | base class for custom types. A subclass sets `name` (text, shown upper-cased as the default metavar) and implements `convert(value, param, ctx)`, which must accept `param=None, ctx=None` and refuses by raising `BadParameter`. It may implement `shell_complete(ctx, param, incomplete)` (section 8) |\n\n## 6. Invocation context\n\n### `Context`\n\nBuilt by the library, one per invocation. The interrupt key raises `KeyboardInterrupt`; the end-of-file key raises `EOFError` |\n| `pause(info=None, err=False)` | |\n| `edit(text=None, editor=None, env=None, require_save=True, extension=\".txt\", filename=None)` | `editor` is a command line. The library runs it with the path of the file to edit among its command-line arguments; the argument position is the implementer’s choice. Returns the saved text as `str`, or `None` (also `None` when `filename` is given) |\n| `launch(url, wait=False, locate=False) -> int` | `url` is a URL or a path. Shell completion\n\n- Variable: `_<PROG>_COMPLETE`, where `<PROG>` is the program name upper-cased with `-` replaced by `_`. `main(complete_var=...)` replaces that name.\n- Values: `<shell>_source` or `<shell>_complete`, with `<shell>` one of `bash`, `zsh`, `fish`, `powershell`.\n- Inputs in complete mode:\n  - `COMP_WORDS` is the command line as one space-joined string, starting with the executable name.\n  - For `bash`, `zsh` and `powershell`, `COMP_CWORD` is the integer index of the incomplete word (equal to the word count when the incomplete token is empty).\n  - For `fish`, `COMP_CWORD` is the incomplete token itself, which may be empty.\n- Output on standard output, after which the process exits with status 0:\n  - Source mode prints the registration script.\n  - Complete mode prints the suggestions. Each suggested value appears verbatim. For `zsh` and `fish`, a suggestion’s help text appears too. A path request is a non-value entry that carries the incomplete token and is of one of two kinds, a directories-only request or a file/any-path request; the two kinds are distinguishable from each other, in a form that is the implementer’s choice. Script syntax, entry framing and separators are the implementer’s choice.\n- Completion functions:\n  - `shell_complete(ctx, param, incomplete)` on an option, or the same method on a custom `ParamType`.\n  - `ctx.params` holds the values already parsed, `param` is the parameter object, and `incomplete` is a `str`.\n  - It returns a list whose items are `str`, or objects exposing `value` (`str`), `help` (`str` or `None`) and `type` (`\"plain\"` for an ordinary value; any other `type` value and its meaning are the implementer’s choice).\n\n## 9. {"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_01JJjRggQa4HXQg9adP6i1tZ","type":"tool_result","content":"1\t# Optlyn — Full Product Requirements Document\n2\t\n3\t## Product overview\n4\t\n5\t**Optlyn** is a Python package for creating command line interfaces in a composable way with as little code as necessary. It is the “Command Line Interface Composition Kit”: highly configurable, with sensible defaults. It exists so that writing command line tools is quick, and so that an intended command-line API can actually be implemented — including arbitrary nesting of commands — rather than being blocked by the parser.\n6\t\n7\tOptlyn in three points, as the product itself states them:\n8\t\n9\t- Arbitrary nesting of commands\n10\t- Automatic help page generation\n11\t- Support for lazy loading of subcommands at runtime\n12\t\n13\tThe finished product is a **library**, not a command users type. An application author declares commands, groups, options, and arguments; Optlyn parses the process argument list, converts values, generates help, dispatches to the author’s callbacks, and supplies terminal helpers. End users of those applications see a POSIX-style command line: options, positional arguments, nested subcommands, and a help page.\n14\t\n15\tThis document specifies **user- and integrator-observable behavior only**. Exact published symbol names, import paths, and decorator spellings belong in the Interface Contract, not here. Every feature point below corresponds to behavior that exists in the finished product. Feature points are ordered so foundational capabilities come first; a later feature point may refine an earlier one only when it says so explicitly.\n16\t\n17\t## Terminology\n18\t\n19\t| Term | Meaning in this PRD |\n20\t| --- | --- |\n21\t| **Command** | A callable unit that parses a slice of the command line and runs an author-supplied callback. A bare command is a leaf: it has options and arguments, but no nested subcommands. |\n22\t| **Group** | A command that dispatches to named subcommands (which may themselves be groups). Groups are how Optlyn nests CLIs. |\n23\t| **Option** | A named parameter, typically introduced by a dash prefix (`-` or `--`, or another declared prefix). Options are optional unless the author marks them required. They appear fully on the help page. |\n24\t| **Argument** | A positional parameter. Arguments are the usual place for files, URLs, and leftover tokens. They are not fully documented on the help page unless the author supplies help text or documents them in the command’s description. |\n25\t| **Parameter** | An option or an argument. |\n26\t| **Invocation context** | The per-invocation state Optlyn creates when a command runs: parsed values, parent/child linkage, an optional author object, resource cleanup, and flags that affect parsing and output. |\n27\t| **Help page** | The usage text Optlyn generates for a command or group when the user asks for help, or when a group is invoked incorrectly under the default “no arguments means help” policy. Layout is Optlyn’s; wording of descriptions is the author’s. |\n28\t| **Callback** | The author function attached to a command, group, or parameter. Command callbacks receive converted parameter values. Parameter callbacks receive the converted value and may replace it or refuse it. A parameter callback is not called for a parameter that was omitted and received no value from any source. |\n29\t| **Eager parameter** | A parameter that can finish the invocation even when other required parameters are still missing. Help and version flags are eager. If several eager flags appear, the one the user typed first is the one that takes effect. |\n30\t| **Default map** | A nested mapping of parameter defaults supplied on the invocation context, used to override declared defaults (for example from a config file) without changing the command definition. |\n31\t| **Chaining group** | A group that runs several subcommands in one invocation, in the order they appear on the command line. |\n32\t| **Interactive session** | A run whose standard input is attached to a terminal (PTY), or whose standard input or standard output is a TTY. A piped standard input without a terminal is not interactive. |\n33\t\n34\t## Public surface inventory\n35\t\n36\tOptlyn is imported and used from Python. The public surface, grouped by feature point, is:\n37\t\n38\t- Declaring a function as a command or a group, attaching options and arguments, registering subcommands immediately or later, and invoking the result as a program or as an in-process call.\n39\t- Automatic help (default `--help`) and an eager version flag that prints a version identity and exits, including a variant whose identity text is produced by an author callback.\n40\t- Built-in parameter types, listed under FP-05; custom types the author supplies.\n41\t- Prompts (option-integrated and standalone), confirmation, and hidden password input, including the ready-made password and confirmation option combinations.\n42\t- File and path parameters, including `-` as stdin/stdout for the file type.\n43\t- Terminal helpers: echo (including to standard error), styling, styled echo, stripping styles, pager output, progress bars, single-character input, pause-until-key, editor launch, application launch, screen clear, application-config directory lookup, filename formatting, text wrapping, and opening files or standard streams.\n44\t- Shell completion for Bash (4.4 and newer), Zsh, Fish, and PowerShell, in both registration-script mode and suggestion-emission mode.\n45\t- Usage-failure and abort handling with distinct exit-status classes.\n46\t- An in-process runner that invokes a command with argument tokens and captures output and exit status.\n47\t\n48\tFeature points below group these entries by capability. They do not invent additional product surfaces. Packaging an application as a console-script entry point is how authors ship tools; it is not itself a Optlyn command.\n49\t\n50\t## Non-functional constraints\n51\t\n52\t- **Form factor:** A pure-Python library. Authors build CLIs with it; Optlyn is not a single end-user binary. The importable package directory is `optlyn` under `src`.\n53\t- **Language:** Python 3.10 or newer. The package has zero declared runtime dependencies. Importing the package performs no I/O, starts no processes, and opens no sockets.\n54\t- **Platforms:** Intended to work on Linux, macOS, and Windows. The supported target is Linux with a supported Python interpreter. No compiled extensions, native code, GPU, or accelerator are required or claimed. (On Windows, when invoked as a program, glob, home-directory, and environment tokens in the process argument list are expanded unless the author disables that; a Unix shell already expands before the process starts.)\n55\t- **Hardware:** CPU-only.\n56\t- **Parsing conventions:** Optlyn implements POSIX-style option parsing (short-option stacking, `--` to end option parsing, long options with `--`). Alternative option prefixes such as `/` and `+` are supported when the author declares them. Leaf commands, by default, also allow an option to appear after a positional argument; groups, by default, do not mix the group’s own options with the subcommand name (FP-03).\n57\t- **Help layout:** Description text is customizable; the help **layout** is not a free-form author template. Nested Optlyn programs keep a consistent help shape when composed.\n58\t- **Unicode:** Command-line values are text. Echo and file helpers exist so misconfigured terminals do not fail on ordinary Unicode output. An ASCII-only environment encoding does not abort invocation (FP-11).\n59\t- **Threading:** The current invocation context is available on the thread that is running the command. Other threads do not see that context unless the author enters the same context in that thread. The context is not a thread-safe mutable store.\n60\t\n61\t## Non-goals\n62\t\n63\t- Being a general-purpose argument parser unrelated to command dispatch (Optlyn both parses and dispatches).\n64\t- Letting authors fully redesign help-page layout (wording yes; layout no).\n65\t- Shipping a remote server, GUI, or web framework.\n66\t- Built-in command aliases or plugin discovery. Those are extension patterns authors implement on top of groups; they are not built-in commands of Optlyn itself. FP-06 requires that custom groups *can* resolve names their own way, not that a particular alias scheme ships.\n67\t- A configuration-file syntax of Optlyn’s own. A default map can be loaded from whatever the author chooses.\n68\t- Thread-safe mutation of an invocation context.\n69\t- Guaranteeing color on every Windows console without extra platform support; recent Windows supports ANSI styling, and echo strips styles when the stream is not a terminal.\n70\t\n71\t---\n72\t\n73\t## Feature points\n74\t\n75\t### FP-01: Command declaration, naming, and invocation\n76\t\n77\t**Public entry:** Optlyn’s command declaration (applied to an ordinary Python function) and invoking the resulting command as a program — by calling it, by running it as a script, or as an installed console script. A group’s command-registration helper is also an entry for attaching a leaf command (FP-06).\n78\t\n79\t**Normal behavior:**\n80\t\n81\t- Decorating a function with no extra arguments produces a command whose name is the function name converted to lowercase, with underscores replaced by dashes, and with a trailing `_command`, `_cmd`, `_group`, or `_grp` suffix stripped when present. Passing an explicit name uses that name instead, and then only that name is accepted: the name derived from the function is not.\n82\t- Invoking the command with a valid argument list runs the function once and returns a successful process exit when used as a program. The function body is the command’s work: whatever it writes appears, and it is not run more than once.\n83\t- A command marked deprecated still runs and still succeeds. On invocation, Optlyn emits a deprecation warning on standard output, ahead of the command’s own output, that is distinguishable from ordinary command output and from a usage failure. A custom deprecation note, when the author supplies one, appears in that warning; the command does not refuse to run merely because it is deprecated. An unknown option on a deprecated command is still a usage error.\n84\t- Parameters declared on the command are converted and passed into the function under the destination names inferred or declared for those parameters (FP-03). A command with no parameters still runs when invoked with an empty extra-argument list. Creating a command or group moves declarations previously attached to the function onto the new command and removes them from the function; decorating the same function again starts from an empty declaration list.\n85\t- When the command is invoked as a standalone program, Optlyn handles the failure classes in FP-13 and exits the process. When the integrator disables standalone program mode, failures propagate to the caller and the command’s return value is available to the caller instead of being discarded.\n86\t\n87\t**Boundary / error behavior:**\n88\t\n89\t- Unknown option tokens, missing required parameters, and values that fail conversion do not run the command callback. They fail as usage errors (FP-13).\n90\t- An ASCII-only environment encoding does not abort execution: the same command still runs and produces the same successful outcome as in a Unicode locale.\n91\t- Leftover tokens beyond the declared arity that no variadic argument collects are a usage error, unless the command is configured to allow extra arguments. With extra arguments allowed, leftover tokens that are not option-shaped are tolerated and the callback runs; each declared argument still receives only the tokens that fill its own arity. An option-shaped leftover token (a leading dash, not after `--`) remains a usage error under that setting alone; consuming it as an argument requires the ignore-unknown-options setting (FP-03) or a preceding `--`.\n92\t\n93\t---\n94\t\n95\t### FP-02: Automatic help pages and eager documentation flags\n96\t\n97\t**Public entry:** The automatic help option on every command (default `--help`, overridable through the invocation context’s help-option names); the command’s docstring and per-option / per-argument help text; the ready-made version option and the ready-made custom-version option; optional epilog, short-help override, metavar, show-default, and show-environment-variable switches.\n98\t\n99\t**Normal behavior:**\n100\t\n101\t- Asking for help on a command prints a help page and does **not** run the command callback. The page includes a usage line, the command’s description, and a documented options section. Intentional help exits successfully (exit status zero).\n102\t- If the function has a docstring, that docstring is the command description, unless the author supplies an explicit help string. A form-feed character in the docstring truncates the help: text after that character is omitted from the help page; text before it remains. The form-feed character itself does not appear on the page.\n103\t- Option help strings appear next to those options. Argument help, when the author supplies it, appears in a positional-arguments section; without it, that section does not carry the argument. Arguments may also be described in the docstring by name.\n104\t- For subcommands listed on a group help page, the short help is the first sentence of the docstring by default, ellipsized if it cannot fit on one line at the wrap width, or an explicit short-help string when the author sets one (which then replaces the first sentence).\n105\t- Group help lists subcommands, the group’s options, positional arguments, and an epilog when one is set. The epilog is printed at the end of the help page, after everything else on it.\n106\t- The usage line brackets optional elements and leaves required elements unbracketed. A variadic argument is marked with a trailing ellipsis. The default options placeholder is bracketed and occupies its own place on the usage line, distinct from any argument placeholder; an author override of that placeholder is used as given, without added brackets. A group that can run without a subcommand also brackets the leading command token; a chaining group brackets the extra command-and-args unit as optional and repeatable.\n107\t- Help text is rewrapped to the terminal width; a maximum content width that defaults to 80 columns and can be raised by the caller caps auto-detected width only, and an explicit caller-supplied terminal width is the wrap width as-is (whatever the maximum content width). Single newlines inside a paragraph are not preserved as hard breaks. A paragraph whose first line is only a backspace character is not rewrapped: subsequent lines of that paragraph keep their line breaks, and the backspace line itself is stripped from the rendered help.\n108\t- The default metavar for an argument is the argument name in uppercase. For an option that takes a value, the default metavar is the type name in uppercase, unless that type supplies its own placeholder (a choice type does); for example, an integer option `--count` appears on the help page as `--count COUNT`; a flag or counting option has no metavar. Authors may override the usage-line options placeholder and per-parameter metavars; an author metavar replaces the type-name placeholder.\n109\t- The help entry of an option whose type is a closed choice lists the allowed values; an option of the plain text type does not.\n110\t- When show-default is enabled, the help page shows the default in that option’s entry. Show-default may be enabled per parameter or for the whole invocation via the context. The author may supply a custom default description, shown instead of the raw default value. For a single-option boolean flag whose default is off (false), that default remains hidden even if show-default is on; a flag whose default is on (true) shows it. When show-environment-variable is enabled, the associated environment variable name appears in that option’s entry; when disabled, it does not.\n111\t- The help page of a deprecated command carries a deprecation mark that the page of an otherwise identical non-deprecated command does not.\n112\t- Hidden options, hidden commands, and hidden groups are omitted from help (and from completion — FP-12) but remain invocable if the user types their names.\n113\t- Help-option names default to `--help`. The invocation context may replace that list; the new names then print help and a name no longer in the list is an unknown option. If an author-declared option reuses every help-option name, the automatic help option is dropped and the author’s option wins; if it reuses only some of those names, the overlapping name runs the author’s option and the remaining names still print help. A parameter merely *named* `help` (for example a positional argument called `help`) does not disable automatic help: both keep working. Authors may also attach an extra help option that prints help and exits the same way as the automatic option; it does not remove the automatic one.\n114\t- The ready-made version option is eager: it prints a version identity and exits without running the command callback, even when other required parameters are missing or present. If the author supplies the version string, the identity contains it. If the author does not supply it, Optlyn detects it from the installed distribution of the given package name; if that name is not an installed distribution, it is treated as an import name and the version of the distribution that provides that import is used. A module’s own version attribute is not consulted. The ready-made custom-version option is the same eager flag, except the whole printed identity is exactly the string returned by an author callback that receives the invocation context: that return value is printed as-is, not wrapped in the built-in package/prog/version template or any other surrounding label. If both help and version appear on the command line, whichever eager flag the user typed first wins and exits; the other’s output does not appear.\n115\t\n116\t**Boundary / error behavior:**\n117\t\n118\t- Help shown because the user invoked a group with no subcommand under the default “no arguments means help” policy is a **usage failure**, not a successful help request: the help page is printed, the group callback is not run (unless the group is configured to invoke without a command — FP-06), and the exit status is the usage-error class (FP-13), not zero.\n119\t- Incorrect usage of a command that causes Optlyn to show help (missing subcommand, and similar no-args-is-help paths) likewise uses the usage-error exit class. Passing the help option explicitly uses the success exit class.\n120\t- A command may disable automatic help. Then `--help` is an unknown option unless the author declared it (for example with an extra help option of that name, which restores it).\n121\t\n122\t---\n123\t\n124\t### FP-03: Options\n125\t\n126\t**Public entry:** Optlyn’s option declaration on a command or group. Ready-made combinations that are still options (password option, confirmation option) are specified under FP-08; the version option under FP-02.\n127\t\n128\t**Normal behavior:**\n129\t\n130\t- Declarations attached as options (or arguments) live on the function until a command or group is created from it: those declarations are then moved onto the new command and removed from the function. Decorating the same function again starts from an empty declaration list. Several options on one command are independent: each fills only its own destination.\n131\t- An option is optional by default. If it is omitted and has no default, the callback receives an absent value. If a default is set, Optlyn infers the type from that default when the author does not set a type (FP-05). A default that is already of the converted type is delivered unchanged. A default may be a callable; that callable is invoked when no earlier value source produced a value.\n132\t- One option may be declared with several names (a short name and a long name, and additional aliases) that all set the same destination. Long options use a double-dash prefix and may take a value as `--name=value` or `--name value`. Short options use a single dash and a single character. Single-character short flags may be stacked: a stack is equivalent to each flag given separately. If the last flag in a stack takes a value, that value may be the next token or attached directly after it, whether alone or at the end of a stack. Multi-character short names are not supported: a single-dash token of several characters is a stack of single-character flags, not one option.\n133\t- When the author does not give a destination name, it is inferred from the declared option names: a name that is already a valid identifier wins; otherwise the first long name; otherwise the first short name. A leading dash prefix is stripped and remaining dashes become underscores.\n134\t- On a leaf command, options and positional arguments may be mixed: an option after an argument is parsed the same as before it. On a group, mixing is off by default: the subcommand name ends that group’s own option parsing, so group options must appear before the subcommand name. Authors may enable mixing on a group, in which case a group option after the subcommand name is still delivered to the group and the subcommand still runs.\n135\t- An option may be required. Then omitting it is a usage error and the callback does not run, unless another source (environment, automatic prefix, default map) supplies it.\n136\t- Boolean flags: a flag declared as a flag, when omitted, yields false unless the author set a true default; when present, it yields true. After `--`, a token spelled like the flag is an argument, not the flag. An explicit on/off pair (declared with either prefix style) yields true for the on token and false for the off token. Several flags may share one destination as a feature-switch group: the callback receives the flag value of the winning flag (see value resolution below).\n137\t- A counting option yields how many times it occurred (zero if omitted). Each flag in a stack counts.\n138\t- A repeatable option may be given several times; the callback receives the sequence of values in command-line order. If it is omitted and has no default, the callback receives an empty tuple, not an absent value. A declared default for a repeatable option must be a sequence (list or tuple) of values, delivered as a tuple in that order when the option is omitted. A multi-value option takes a fixed number of tokens per occurrence (strictly positive; not “consume the rest”): it is delivered as an indexable sequence of that length, a following token is left for the next parameter, and too few tokens is a usage error. Combined with repetition, each occurrence takes that many tokens. A tuple type on an option sets that arity to the tuple length and converts each position with the corresponding inner type.\n139\t- An option may take an optional value: the flag alone yields the author’s flag-value; the flag plus a token yields that token; omitting the flag entirely yields the default. (A value option without this form, given with no value, is a missing-value usage error.)\n140\t- Authors may declare prefixes other than `-`, including `/` and `+`.\n141\t- Environment variables: an option may name one variable or a list of names (first one set wins). Names are matched exactly and are not whitespace-trimmed as names. An absent variable, or a variable present with a truly empty value, is treated as not supplying a value (the next source wins). An environment value is converted with the option’s type and may satisfy a required option. For a repeatable or multi-value option, the type splits a non-empty variable’s string: default split is whitespace; file and path types split on the platform path separator (`:` on Unix), keeping left-to-right order.\n142\t- For boolean flags, environment values are strings interpreted as follows after stripping surrounding whitespace and ignoring case. Activation: `true`, `1`, `yes`, `on`, `t`, `y`. Deactivation: `false`, `0`, `no`, `off`, `f`, `n`. A whitespace-only value strips to empty and deactivates. Any other non-empty string is a conversion usage error, not a silent deactivation. If the flag has a non-boolean flag-value, a variable whose text equals that flag-value also activates; recognized true/false tokens activate or deactivate as above; unrecognized and empty values are treated as unset (the next source wins), not as a usage error. A paired on/off option recognizes only the single environment name the author attached, not a magically derived negative name.\n143\t- A value is filled from command line, then environment, then the default map on the invocation context (FP-07), then the parameter’s declared default; the first of those that produces a value wins. Those four, plus an interactive prompt when one ran (FP-08), are ranked from most explicit to least as: prompt, command line, environment, default map, declared default.\n144\t- Feature-switch groups (several options sharing one destination): the option whose source is most explicit wins. Within the default tier, an explicit declared default beats an auto-derived default (bare boolean flags auto-derive default false). If still tied, the last declared option wins.\n145\t- A parameter callback sees the invocation context, the parameter, and the converted value, and may replace the value or refuse it. A refusal is a usage error: non-zero usage-class exit, a message on standard error that distinguishes the failure from success, the command callback not run, and the refused value not delivered. Callbacks run for every source including environment, default map, and prompts. An eager flag can finish the invocation even when required non-eager options are missing; when it is not given, the missing required option is still a usage error. A missing parameter still runs its callback, so that callback can default from an earlier parameter’s value (the values already bound are readable on the context). A repeated parameter fires its callback once, with all gathered values.\n146\t- A parameter may be hidden from the callback (not passed as a function argument) while still being parsed — used by help, version, and confirmation flags. Its name is still accepted on the command line.\n147\t- A deprecated option still parses. A deprecation warning is emitted only when the user actually supplied that option, not when the value came only from a default.\n148\t\n149\t**Boundary / error behavior:**\n150\t\n151\t- An unknown option is a usage error, unless the command is configured to ignore unknown options, in which case option-like tokens may be consumed as arguments without `--`, and leftover option-like tokens become extra arguments that a variadic pass-through argument can collect (FP-04). Unknown long options are left intact. Unknown short options may be split: a known short flag inside a stack is consumed and the unknown rest of the stack stays leftover. An option-like token left over beyond the declared arity is still a usage error unless extra arguments are allowed (FP-01).\n152\t- A missing value for an option that requires one is a usage error.\n153\t- A bare string (or other non-sequence) default on a repeatable option is a usage error whose report identifies the option and says that it needs an iterable (sequence) default, so that report is distinct from the report for a missing required option; it is not treated as a sequence of characters and not as a single string element. Authors who want one default string must pass a one-element sequence.\n154\t- A deprecated option cannot also be required, and cannot use a prompt. Declaring that combination is refused at declaration time.\n155\t- Option values belonging to a command must appear after that command’s name and before a nested command name (FP-06). A help option before a subcommand name is help for the parent, not for the subcommand.\n156\t\n157\t---\n158\t\n159\t### FP-04: Positional arguments\n160\t\n161\t**Public entry:** Optlyn’s argument declaration on a command or group.\n162\t\n163\t**Normal behavior:**\n164\t\n165\t- An argument is positional and binds tokens in declaration order. A minimal argument (a destination name only) is required, has no default, and is text unless a type or default implies otherwise (an integer default infers integer conversion, as for options).\n166\t- An argument may be marked optional, or given a default; then omitting it is not a usage error and the callback receives the default, or an absent value (neither a string nor a sequence) when there is none. A supplied token overrides a default. An argument may declare a fixed positive arity or a variadic arity (consume the rest). A unary argument is delivered as a scalar; any other arity is delivered as an indexable sequence. Too few tokens for a required fixed arity is a usage error. Variadic arity may be used at most once on a command; a second variadic argument is refused or never runs the callback. A variadic argument omitted yields an empty sequence unless it was marked required, in which case omitting it is a usage error.\n167\t- After a `--` token, subsequent tokens are arguments even if they look like options; the `--` token itself is not delivered. Without it, option-shaped tokens are not arguments (FP-01, FP-03).\n168\t- An argument declared on a group is delivered to the group callback; the next token after it is the subcommand name.\n169\t- Arguments may read from environment variables only when the author names those variables explicitly (one name or a list; first set wins). There is no automatic environment prefix for arguments (that prefix applies to options — FP-07), and a variable merely named like the destination does not fill one. An absent or truly empty variable is treated as not supplying a value. An environment value may satisfy a required argument and is overridden by a command-line token. A non-empty variable for a non-unary argument is split the same way as for a multi-value option (FP-03); a unary argument keeps the whole value.\n170\t- Argument help is optional. Without it, the help page’s main description is where authors document them; with it, a positional-arguments section lists them (FP-02). An author metavar is the argument’s placeholder on the usage line.\n171\t\n172\t**Boundary / error behavior:**\n173\t\n174\t- A missing required argument is a usage error that identifies that argument, and the callback does not run.\n175\t- Extra tokens beyond declared arity, when no variadic argument collects them and extra arguments are not allowed, are a usage error.\n176\t- With ignore-unknown-options enabled, option-shaped tokens may be consumed as arguments without needing `--`.\n177\t- A deprecated argument still parses and cannot be required; an argument with neither a default nor an optional marking counts as required. Declaring that combination is refused at declaration time. A deprecation warning is emitted only when the user actually supplied that argument, not when the value came only from a default.\n178\t\n179\t---\n180\t\n181\t### FP-05: Parameter types and conversion\n182\t\n183\t**Public entry:** The type attached to an option or argument, or inferred from a default. Built-in types are a fixed finite set. Authors may also supply a custom type.\n184\t\n185\t**Normal behavior:**\n186\t\n187\tBuilt-in types:\n188\t\n189\t- **String** — the default; Unicode text. An explicit string type keeps numeric- or boolean-looking tokens as text.\n190\t- **Integer** — only integers (a token with a fractional part is not one); delivered as a Python integer. Conversion failure is a usage error. Inferred from an integer default.\n191\t- **Float** — only floating-point numbers; delivered as a Python float. Inferred from a float default.\n192\t- **Boolean** — used automatically for boolean flags and inferred from a boolean default; delivers a real boolean. Text conversion (case-insensitive) treats `1`, `true`, `t`, `yes`, `y`, `on` as true and `0`, `false`, `f`, `no`, `n`, `off` as false; anything else is a usage error.\n193\t- **UUID** — accepts UUID text and yields a UUID value. It is never inferred automatically from a default.\n194\t- **Choice** — a closed list of allowed values, or the member names of an enumeration. Matching is case-sensitive unless the author turns that off. The value delivered is the original choice object (enumeration member or original list entry), not merely the matched string, even when matching is case-insensitive. If two choices normalize to the same token, the first registered original is delivered. Repeatable choice options are allowed; a default for a repeatable choice must be a sequence of valid choices.\n195\t- **Date-time** — parses into a date-time value. Formats are tried in order; the first success wins. The default format list is the finite set: date `YYYY-MM-DD`; date and time with `T` as `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS`; date and time with a space as `YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS`. Authors may supply their own list of format strings, which replaces the default list (it does not extend it). Values parsed under the defaults are not timezone-aware.\n196\t- **Integer range** — an integer that must lie in an optional minimum/maximum range. Bounds are closed by default; either side may be open (boundary excluded) or omitted (unbounded). With clamp enabled, a value outside the range (including a value equal to an open bound) is replaced by the nearest included value: the included bound itself for a closed bound, and the adjacent integer inside the range for an open bound.\n197\t- **Float range** — the same range rules for floats.
